issues.issue: The grant describes the licensed property as "including, but not limited to, fixtures, existing improvements, and appurtenant structures" and defers to Exhibit A, so the outer boundary of the "Premises" is left open-ended against enumerated specifics. A court could be asked whether anything beyond the listed items and the Exhibit A parcel is licensed.

The open-ended grant sits against Exhibit A, which itself says the Premises "shall include, but is not limited to" a precise metes-and-bounds Parcel No. 3, so neither document fixes what land is covered. The two open-ended descriptions compound rather than resolve each other.

"Hardrives intends to utilize the Premises for ... paving materials and other similar products" is drafted as a statement of intent, not a covenant, leaving it unclear whether it limits permitted use at all, and "other similar products" has no fixed boundary. A court could be asked whether a given activity is a permitted use or a breach.

The written word and the numeral disagree: "thirty (80) days," so the cure/default trigger period is internally contradictory on its face. A court would have to decide whether thirty or eighty days governs the event of default.

The term "shall continue: (1) for a term of one (1) year ... or (2) until the date that title ... is conveyed" joins two inconsistent measures with "or" and gives no rule for which controls, so it is unclear whether the licence expires after a year or runs until conveyance. It also does not say what happens if the contemplated Development Agreement is never entered into by December 31, 1999.

The clause presupposes a separate Development Agreement conveying title, yet paragraph 9 declares this Agreement and documents delivered pursuant to it the entire agreement, leaving the relationship between the two instruments unresolved. A court could be asked whether the licence survives once the Development Agreement path fails.

The warranty that the Premises "shall be clear of all liens and claims of any party" is qualified by an enumerated list of exceptions (easements of record, unrecorded easements identified by the City, rights of way, Center Street Bridge access rights) whose reach is uncertain, particularly "any and all unrecorded easements identified by the City prior to the execution." Whether an unlisted encumbrance falls inside or outside the carve-out is a construction question.

The flat statement that "there are no claims, actions, suits, or proceedings ... which may affect the Premises" is hard to square with paragraph 6.D's acknowledgement of conditions disclosed in the Exhibit B environmental assessment and with Exhibit A's excepted conveyances to CSX and Mahoning County. A court could be asked whether those disclosures qualify this warranty.

"All easements and right of ways, as may be necessary to have access to, and utilization of, the Premises" fixes no identified easements and no standard of necessity, so its scope is indeterminate. A court would have to decide what access rights the licence actually conveys.

This grant of "all easements and right of ways ... necessary" sits awkwardly against paragraph 6.B, which excepts rights of way and access rights appurtenant to the Center Street Bridge and ramps from the City's clear-title warranty. The two provisions point in opposite directions on the same access rights.

The syntax buries the qualifier: the Premises has never contained hazardous materials "except as set forth in the Environmental Site Assessment ... in violation of any applicable environmental laws or regulations," so it is unreadable whether the warranty is of no contamination at all, no contamination beyond the report, or only no unlawful contamination. That misplaced modifier is the whole measure of the City's environmental exposure.

The exception incorporates the Exhibit B Phase I/II assessment, which describes "Parcel No. 3" as a 5.44-acre site within a 123.07-acre study area, while Exhibit A's Parcel No. 3 is a 58.086-acre tract from the LTV quit claim deed. The disclosure document and the definition of the Premises do not describe the same land, so the scope of the carve-out cannot be fixed from the instrument.

"Lay no waste" and return "in as good a condition as received, normal wear and tear and damage due to casualty excepted" set no measurable baseline for a contaminated former steel site. What condition the Premises was "received" in is precisely what the parties would dispute.

The obligation to surrender the Premises substantially unaltered is hard to reconcile with paragraph 2, which contemplates industrial production, distribution and storage of paving materials and equipment on the site. A court could be asked whether use authorised by paragraph 2 can constitute waste under this paragraph.

"All precautions necessary to ensure against the creation, use, or storage of any hazardous material" is an absolute-sounding standard with no benchmark, and the second sentence limits compliance to "Environmental Protection Agency laws or regulations" only. Whether Ohio EPA/ORC obligations or common-law duties fall inside that phrase is open.

This narrow undertaking to comply with "Environmental Protection Agency laws or regulations" sits against paragraph 7.F, which requires conformity with all applicable federal, state and local laws, leaving Hardrives' environmental compliance duty stated at two different widths. A court would have to decide which measure governs contamination claims.

The indemnity covers claims "resulting from injury on or about the Premises or in conjunction with Hardrives' use and occupancy," without saying whether "injury" reaches environmental contamination and cleanup costs or only bodily/property injury, and without any carve-out for the City's own fault. Both the subject matter and the party protected are open to construction.

A broad indemnity running to the City is difficult to square with paragraph 6.D, in which the City warrants the environmental condition of the Premises, if the same contamination is both warranted against and indemnified. A court could be asked which provision allocates pre-existing contamination liability.

The general compliance covenant overlaps paragraph 7.D's narrower Environmental Protection Agency compliance obligation, and it is unclear whether the specific environmental clause qualifies this general one. The tension is mild but nameable.

The "as is" acceptance with no express or implied warranty is expressly subject to "warranties and representations made by the City ... contained in this Agreement," which include the paragraph 6.D environmental warranty; the two provisions point in opposite directions on the condition of the Premises. A court would have to decide how much of the as-is disclaimer survives paragraph 6.D.

The merger clause makes this Agreement and "the documents delivered pursuant hereto" the entire agreement, yet paragraph 5 conditions the term on a separate Development Agreement to be entered into later. Whether that later instrument is inside or outside the integration is a construction question.

The bar on assignment without written consent stands against paragraph 12, which extends the defined terms "City" and "Hardrives" to their "successors, and assigns." A court could be asked whether paragraph 12 contemplates assignees the assignment clause forbids.

The survival clause says warranties survive "the execution and delivery of this Agreement" but says nothing about surviving termination or expiry of the one-year term. Whether the City's environmental warranty remains enforceable after the licence ends is left open.

Including "assigns" within the defined parties is in tension with paragraph 9's prohibition on assignment without written consent. The definition appears to contemplate a class the operative clause bars.

A precise metes-and-bounds description of Parcel No. 3 is prefaced by "shall include, but is not limited to," so the survey does not close the definition of the Premises. A court would have to decide whether land outside the described bounds is licensed.

The 58.086-acre Parcel No. 3 described here does not match the "Parcel No. 3 (5.44 acre site)" assessed in the Exhibit B environmental report incorporated by paragraph 6.D. The two exhibits use the same parcel label for different land.

The excepted conveyances to CSX and Mahoning County sit against paragraph 6.B's warranty that the Premises is clear of all liens and claims and that no proceedings affect it, and against Exhibit A's "not limited to" language. Whether these exceptions qualify the City's warranty is left unstated.
